title: Switched On: How Life Changed
summary: Once electricity arrived, it changed almost everything. Electric trams replaced horses, lifts carried people up skyscrapers, and machines like vacuum cleaners, fridges and washing machines took over heavy chores at home. Radio, cinema, bright city streets and even X-rays that could see inside the body all ran on electricity.

sections.heading: All Aboard the Electric Train
paragraphs: Imagine visiting the Berlin trade exhibition in 1879. Among the machines and stands you spot a crowd queuing for a ride. A tiny locomotive, not much bigger than a garden shed on wheels, is pulling open carriages full of laughing visitors around a short track. There is no smoke, no hissing steam, no coal. The power comes through an extra rail on the ground. This was the world's first electric passenger train, built by Werner von Siemens and his company, Siemens and Halske.

Siemens knew it was more than a fairground ride. In May 1881 his company opened the world's first electric tram service in Gross-Lichterfelde, a suburb of Berlin. In 1882 he even tested an electric bus called the Elektromote, which took its power from overhead wires, an early ancestor of the trolleybus.

Across the Atlantic, the man who made electric streetcars a real success was Frank Julian Sprague, a former US Navy officer who had worked briefly with Thomas Edison. In 1887 he took on a job that many thought impossible: to build a complete electric tram system in Richmond, Virginia, a hilly city with steep slopes and sharp curves. After trials in late 1887, regular service began on 2 February 1888 with 10 streetcars.

Each car drew power at 450 volts from an overhead wire, through a pole on its roof, and had two electric motors. The big cars had 40 seats and could carry up to 100 passengers, cruising at about 12 kilometres per hour with a top speed around 24. By June 1888 the system had 40 cars running on about 19 kilometres of track. In September 1888 officials from Boston came to inspect it and decided to build a similar system at home.

What happened next was one of the fastest changes in transport history. Before electricity, most city trams were pulled by horses. Horses were slow, needed huge stables, got tired, fell ill and left tonnes of manure in the streets every day. By 1895, only about seven years after Richmond, the United States had almost 900 electric street railways with nearly 18,000 kilometres of track, and horse-drawn street railways had almost disappeared within a little over a decade. Electric trams let cities spread outwards, because workers could now live in new suburbs and ride into town every morning.

Electricity went underground too. Early underground railways, like London's first lines from 1863, used steam engines, which filled tunnels with smoke. On 18 December 1890 the City and South London Railway opened to the public. It ran deep below the streets in round iron tunnels, the first successful deep-level tube railway in the world, and its trains were pulled by electric locomotives. The first line was about 5 kilometres long with six stations, and every journey cost a flat twopence. Its small, windowless carriages were nicknamed padded cells, but people loved the speed: about 5.1 million passengers rode it in its first year. Nearly every big city's metro since then has run on electricity.

sections.heading: Going Up: Lifts and Tall Buildings
paragraphs: Before lifts, which Americans call elevators, there was a limit to how tall a useful building could be. Nobody wanted to climb ten flights of stairs to reach an office, so the top floors of tall buildings were cheap and often empty. Lifting goods with ropes and pulleys was old, but carrying people safely was another matter, because everyone feared what would happen if the rope snapped.

Elisha Otis solved the fear first. In 1852 he introduced a safety brake that would grab the guide rails if the lifting cable broke, and in 1854 he showed it off dramatically at the New York Crystal Palace exhibition. In 1857 the first passenger lift was installed at 488 Broadway in New York, in the Haughwout Building. These early lifts were powered by steam engines and later by water pressure, called hydraulic lifts.

Electricity made lifts faster, simpler and easier to put into any building. In 1880 Werner von Siemens, busy as ever, built the first electric lift in Germany. Frank Sprague, fresh from his Richmond trams, developed electric lifts too, which could go faster and carry larger loads than hydraulic or steam ones. He installed 584 of them before selling his company to the Otis Elevator Company in 1895.

Together with strong steel frames, electric lifts made the skyscraper possible. In the early 1900s New York and Chicago began to rise upward, with buildings of 20, 40 and then more than 100 storeys. The Empire State Building, finished in 1931 with 102 storeys, depended completely on its banks of electric lifts. Without electricity there could be no modern city skyline.

sections.heading: Factories Without Belts
paragraphs: Step inside a big factory in the 1880s and you would hear a deafening clatter and feel the floor trembling. Somewhere in the building was a single huge steam engine. It turned a long iron rod called a line shaft that ran along the ceiling of every workshop. From the line shaft, dozens of leather belts dropped down to each machine below, flapping and slapping as they spun. If the steam engine stopped, every machine in the factory stopped. If you wanted to use just one machine, the whole engine still had to run.

These belt systems were also dangerous. A loose sleeve or a ponytail caught by a moving belt could drag a worker into the machinery. The rooms were often dim, because the windows had to fit around the shafts, and gas lamps or oil lamps were a fire risk in buildings full of cotton, wood or oil.

Electric motors changed all of that, though it took several decades. At first factories simply replaced the big steam engine with one big electric motor, keeping the belts. Then engineers realised they could give each machine its own small motor. This was called unit drive. Now a machine could be switched on and off by itself, placed anywhere on the floor, and moved when needed. Factories no longer had to be built around the line shaft. They could be laid out to follow the order of the work, one step after another, which made assembly lines much easier to design.

Electric motors were several times more efficient than small steam engines, because the power came from big, efficient central power stations and there was much less energy lost to friction in shafts and belts. The amount of mechanical power available to each American worker grew enormously, from about half a horsepower for each worker in the 1870s to about five horsepower by 1950. By about 1925, half of the power used by industry came from central power stations rather than a factory's own engines.

Electric light changed factories too. Bright, steady lamps meant fewer accidents and less eye strain, and they made it much easier to run a night shift. Some factories began to run around the clock, which helped produce more goods but also meant that more people worked through the night. Electricity made products cheaper, from cars to clothing to tinned food, and that would soon fill people's homes with new things to buy, many of them electric.

sections.heading: The Electric Servants Move In
paragraphs: Now walk into a home in about 1900, before most houses had electricity. Housework was exhausting. On washing day, which usually took the whole day, water had to be carried and heated on a stove, clothes were soaked, scrubbed on a ridged washboard, rinsed, wrung out by hand or through a mangle, and hung up to dry. Then came ironing with solid metal irons, called sad irons, heated on the stove. You kept several, swapping a hot one for the one that had gone cold. Carpets were dragged outside and beaten with a stick. Food had to be bought almost every day because there was no good way to keep it cold. Most of this work was done by women and girls, or by servants in richer homes.

Electric appliances started to appear surprisingly early, even before many homes could use them. In the early 1880s Schuyler Wheeler in New York designed an electric fan, and in 1882 Philip Diehl made one of the first electric ceiling fans. Also in 1882, on 6 June, Henry W. Seeley of New York patented an electric iron. It weighed almost 7 kilograms and took a long time to heat up, and of course you needed electricity at home to use it, which very few people had. Irons with a thermostat, a switch that keeps the temperature steady, arrived in the 1920s, so you no longer had to guess whether you were about to scorch your shirt.

The vacuum cleaner has a famous story. In London around 1901 an engineer named Hubert Cecil Booth watched a demonstration of a machine that tried to clean by blowing dust away, which mostly just moved it around. He wondered whether sucking would work better. To test it, he reportedly put a handkerchief over the seat of a restaurant chair, pressed his mouth to it and sucked hard. When he looked, the cloth was dirty on the underside. Booth patented his cleaner in 1901. His first big machine, nicknamed Puffing Billy, was actually driven by a petrol engine and pulled through the streets by horses. It parked outside a building while long hoses went in through the windows. Booth soon made electric versions, and in the following decades smaller electric vacuum cleaners that one person could push around a room became common.

Refrigerators took longer. Before them, many families had an icebox, a wooden cupboard lined with metal, where a block of ice delivered by the iceman kept food cool for a day or two. Some of the first electric home refrigerators, made by Fred Wolf in Fort Wayne, Indiana, from about 1913, sat on top of an ordinary icebox. Kelvinator and Frigidaire both started selling refrigerators in 1918, but they were very expensive. In 1922 one model cost 714 dollars, more than a Ford Model T car at about 476 dollars. In 1927 General Electric launched the Monitor-Top, with its round machinery perched on top like a hat, for 525 dollars. Over a million were made. Refrigerators meant less shopping, less food going bad, and fewer people falling ill from spoiled food.

Electric washing machines were being advertised in American newspapers by 1904. Many early ones were a tub with an electric motor that swished the clothes about, plus a powered wringer, two rollers that squeezed out the water, which could catch fingers and was quite dangerous. Sales grew fast: about 800,000 electric washers were sold in the United States in 1928. By 1940, about 60 per cent of the 25 million American homes wired for electricity had an electric washing machine. In 1937 the Bendix company introduced the first automatic home washing machine. Early versions had to be bolted to the floor because they shook so much when spinning.

These machines did not get rid of housework, but they changed it. Jobs that had taken a whole day could take an hour or two. Historians point out that standards also rose, so people started washing clothes more often and expecting cleaner homes. Still, electric appliances gave millions of people, especially women, more time and less heavy lifting. They also changed how houses were built, with sockets in every room. In the United States about 70 per cent of homes were electrified by 1930, mainly in towns and cities, while many farms, as we saw in the last part, had to wait longer.

sections.heading: Voices, Music and Moving Pictures
paragraphs: Electricity did not only do work. It brought entertainment and news into homes, and it made new kinds of entertainment possible.

The telephone, patented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, carried voices as electrical signals along wires. By the early 1900s, telephone wires were strung through every city, and switchboard operators, most of them young women, connected calls by plugging cords into sockets.

Radio came next. Radio waves are the invisible electromagnetic waves first produced by Heinrich Hertz, which we met in Part 6. On the evening of 2 November 1920, the Westinghouse company broadcast the results of the American presidential election from East Pittsburgh. Perhaps a thousand people listened. It was not the only station on the air that night, and historians still argue about which station deserves to be called the first true broadcaster, but the event helped start a radio craze. Within a few years millions of families gathered around radio sets in the evening for news, music, comedy and sport. In Britain the BBC began broadcasting in 1922.

The cinema depended on electricity too. A projector needed a very bright lamp to throw images onto a large screen, and electric motors to run the film smoothly. In 1927 the film The Jazz Singer became famous as one of the first feature films with synchronised talking scenes, using electrical sound recording and loudspeakers. Picture palaces with thousands of seats opened in cities around the world, glowing with electric signs outside.

Television combined many of these ideas. In January 1926 the Scottish inventor John Logie Baird demonstrated a working television system in London, using a spinning disc. Electronic television, using cathode-ray tubes, soon proved better. The BBC began a regular high-definition television service from Alexandra Palace in London in 1936, although only a few thousand people had sets at first. After the Second World War, television spread rapidly, and by the 1960s it had become the centre of the living room in many countries. Every one of these inventions, from the telephone to the television, needed a steady supply of electricity, either from a battery or, increasingly, from the grid.

sections.heading: The Night Comes Alive
paragraphs: For all of human history, night had been dark, and dangerous. Gas streetlights had helped, but they were dim. Electric lighting turned city streets into places where people could walk, shop and meet late into the evening.

New York's Broadway became famous for its blazing lights and was nicknamed the Great White Way. In 1904 Longacre Square was renamed Times Square, after the New York Times moved its headquarters there, and about three weeks later the first electric advertisement appeared on a building there. By the 1920s advertisers were spending tens of millions of dollars a year on giant signs that flashed and moved using thousands of bulbs. One huge sign for Wrigley's Spearmint chewing gum, possibly the biggest electric sign of its time, cost 9,000 dollars a month to rent.

Even celebrations changed. In 1904, 1905 and 1906, New Year was marked with fireworks from the roof of the Times building, but city officials stopped them because of the fire danger. So on 31 December 1907 the famous ball drop began instead: a lit ball lowered down a pole at midnight. It still happens every year, though today the ball is covered in LEDs.

Electric light made roads safer, helped police and changed shops, which could now light up their windows for people passing by in the evening. Night life grew, with restaurants, dance halls, cinemas and theatres open late. Sports could be played after dark under floodlights. Shift workers, nurses, bakers and printers could work through the night in good light. Little by little, the old rhythm of going to bed soon after sunset faded away. That brought freedom and fun, but, as later parts of this story show, it also had costs, including the bright glow that now hides the stars from most city dwellers.

sections.heading: Seeing Inside the Body
paragraphs: Some of the most important electric inventions were in medicine and science. One of the most amazing came from a German physicist named Wilhelm Röntgen at the University of Würzburg.

On 8 November 1895 Röntgen was experimenting with a glass tube from which most of the air had been pumped out, called a Crookes tube. When a high voltage was applied, an electrical discharge passed through it. He had covered the tube with black cardboard so no light could escape. Yet across the room, a screen painted with a chemical called barium platinocyanide began to glow. Something invisible was coming out of the tube, passing through the cardboard and lighting up the screen. Not knowing what it was, he called it X, the letter scientists use for an unknown, and the name X-rays stuck.

Röntgen worked secretly for weeks to study the rays. He found that they passed through paper, wood and flesh but were blocked by bones and metal. One of the first X-ray photographs he made, dated 22 December 1895, shows the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, with her bones and her ring clearly visible. His first paper appeared on 28 December 1895. The news spread around the world within weeks, and doctors were soon using X-rays to find broken bones and swallowed objects, and bullets in wounded soldiers. In 1901 Röntgen received the first ever Nobel Prize in Physics. He refused to patent his discovery, because he wanted everyone to be able to benefit from it.

At first nobody realised that X-rays could also be harmful in large doses, and some early researchers were injured before safety rules were developed. Today doctors use them carefully, with protective screens and the smallest dose needed.

Hospitals filled with other electrical equipment too. Electric lights made operating theatres far brighter than gas or candles ever could. In the early 1900s the Dutch physiologist Willem Einthoven built a sensitive instrument that could record the tiny electrical signals of the beating heart, the electrocardiogram or ECG, and he won the Nobel Prize for it in 1924. It is a fitting link back to Galvani's twitching frogs: our bodies really do run on electrical signals. In 1928 the Drinker respirator, an electrically powered iron lung, helped people breathe when their muscles were paralysed. Electricity had become part of saving lives.

sections.heading: Selling the Electric Dream
paragraphs: Having electricity in the house was one thing. Persuading people to use it was another. In the early days many homes were wired only for lights, with perhaps one socket, and some families plugged appliances into the light fitting hanging from the ceiling. Electricity was still expensive, and lots of people did not trust it. Would it give you a shock? Would it set the curtains on fire? Was it worth the money?

Power companies had a strong reason to win them over. A power station built for evening lighting sat mostly idle during the day, while its owners still had to pay for the machines. Every iron, fan, washing machine or refrigerator used during daylight hours meant more income from the same equipment. So electricity companies and appliance makers began advertising heavily. Newspapers and magazines filled with pictures of smiling families and spotless kitchens. Showrooms let people try appliances before buying them, and many families paid in small monthly instalments, a system known in Britain as hire purchase.

Some of the most effective campaigners were women engineers. In Britain the Electrical Association for Women was founded in 1924, with the engineer Caroline Haslett as its first director. It ran cookery demonstrations, published advice, and taught women how electricity worked and how to use it safely, arguing that electric power could free women from drudgery. Similar groups and demonstration homes appeared in other countries.

Houses began to be designed differently. Builders added more sockets, wired kitchens for electric cookers, and left space for a refrigerator. Exhibitions showed off all-electric homes where everything, from the kettle to the heating, ran from the mains. By the 1950s and 1960s, in many richer countries, a house without a fridge, a television and a vacuum cleaner was starting to seem old-fashioned. The demand from all these homes in turn pushed power companies to build ever bigger stations and grids, the giant system described in the last part. Homes and the grid grew together, each one driving the other.

Think how much changed in a single lifetime. A child born in 1880 grew up with candles, oil lamps, horse-drawn trams and washing day by hand. If that child lived to 1960, they could ride an electric underground train, take a lift to the top of a skyscraper, store food in a refrigerator, listen to the radio, watch television and have an X-ray at the hospital. Electricity had moved from being a scientific wonder to something people barely noticed, until it stopped working.

And that is the warning at the end of this part. All this power came with hidden costs. Wires could give deadly shocks and start fires. Power stations poured out smoke. And when a grid failed, whole cities could be plunged into sudden darkness. The next part looks at the dark side of the electric age.

deepDive: Economic historians have long puzzled over a strange delay. Electric motors were available in the 1880s, yet American factory productivity did not jump dramatically until the 1920s. The economist Paul David famously compared this to computers, which spread through offices for years before they clearly raised productivity. His explanation was that simply swapping a steam engine for an electric motor changed little. The real gains came only when factories were redesigned from scratch around unit drive: single-storey buildings, machines placed in the order of the work, better light and ventilation, and flexible layouts. That required new buildings, new managers and new habits, which took a generation. By the time central power stations supplied about half of industrial power in the mid-1920s, the transformation was well under way. Historians also debate the household story. Ruth Schwartz Cowan, in her book More Work for Mother (1983), argued that electric appliances did not reduce the total hours many housewives spent on housework as much as advertisers promised, because expectations of cleanliness rose, servants disappeared from middle-class homes, and tasks once sent out to laundries returned to the home. Other researchers have found that appliances did free up time and helped more women take paid jobs, especially after the Second World War. Both effects can be true at once, and they varied between rich and poor families and between countries. There was also a business logic behind the appliance boom: power stations built for evening lighting stood half idle by day, so utilities promoted daytime loads such as irons, washers and motors to spread their fixed costs, a measure engineers call the load factor. Finally, electrification spread very unevenly. In 1930 about 70 per cent of American homes had electricity, yet most farms did not, and in many parts of the world the electric revolution described in this part did not reach ordinary homes until much later in the twentieth century, or has still not arrived. The changes were real and enormous, but they did not arrive for everyone at the same time.
funFact: Hubert Cecil Booth's first big vacuum cleaner of 1901, nicknamed Puffing Billy, was not electric at all: it ran on a petrol engine and was pulled through London's streets by horses.
